interview_metadata.name: Raki Roseberry
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Indianapolis, mostly around the east side, with a lot of family history tied to the Indiana Avenue corridor. I grew up in a Black church family where Sundays meant service, somebody cooking, gospel music on, and grown folks telling stories at the table. My mom worked in health care administration and my dad did maintenance work, so I learned early that steady work matters, but I also saw how stress sits in people's bodies. I was a quiet, observant kid, good in school, the one who organized her notebooks by color and worried if a plan changed. After high school I went to Ivy Tech and earned an Associate of Applied Science in Massage Therapy. I did not take the straightest path emotionally, because I had anxiety and some money pressure, but bodywork gave me a calling. I became a licensed massage therapist, built up a client list, and now I do deep tissue, myofascial, sports massage, and lymphatic drainage. I have never been married and I do not have children. A lot of my adult life has been learning how to care for other people without forgetting to care for myself. These days I am working, training for runs, doing yoga, listening to jazz, cooking, and slowly planning a wellness center for Black and underserved neighborhoods in Indianapolis.

follow_ups.question: What is one childhood memory that still shapes how you see community?
follow_ups.response: I remember family dinners after church where neighbors came through even if they were not blood family. Somebody always had a plate, and that taught me that care is practical, not just something you say.

follow_ups.question: Who was most influential when you were deciding what kind of work to do?
follow_ups.response: My mother influenced me because she understood the medical system, but my aunt Denise really pushed me toward massage. She had chronic back pain, and I saw how much relief skilled touch could give her.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes. My biggest crossroads was after I finished some general classes and was deciding whether to stay in a regular office track or go into massage therapy. I had been working front-desk jobs and could have stayed in administration because it felt safer. But I was also taking yoga, reading about stress, and seeing people in my family deal with pain, blood pressure, grief, and tension without enough support. I visited a massage program at Ivy Tech and watched a student assessment, and something clicked. It looked clinical and personal at the same time. I chose the massage therapy program even though it meant student debt, awkward schedules, and explaining to family that this was real health work. That decision gave me a professional identity.

follow_ups.question: What made the safer office path tempting?
follow_ups.response: It had predictable pay and benefits. My family respects stability, so I felt pressure to choose something with a clear paycheck every two weeks.

follow_ups.question: What did you do first after deciding on massage therapy?
follow_ups.response: I met with an advisor, mapped out my classes, and started saving for supplies like sheets, oils, textbooks, and scrubs.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was definitely conscious. I made a spreadsheet with program costs, work hours, licensing steps, and what I thought I could earn.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help you think it through?
follow_ups.response: My mom talked through the practical side with me, and my aunt Denise encouraged me from the heart side.

follow_ups.question: Do you still make decisions that way?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I still plan things out. I can be anxious, so having numbers and steps calms me down.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. More career counseling and scholarships for allied health students would have helped. I figured out licensing, business basics, and financial aid mostly by asking around.

follow_ups.question: What support would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A mentor who already owned a practice would have saved me mistakes with pricing, taxes, and client boundaries.

follow_ups.question: Did any organization help at all?
follow_ups.response: Ivy Tech helped academically, and local massage therapists were generous once I started networking.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now and I do not have children. I have never been married. My family is still very important to me, especially my mother, Angela, who lives in Indianapolis, and my younger brother Marcus, who is across town with his wife and two kids. My dad, Robert, is around too, though we are not as emotionally close as I am with my mom. I check on my mother several times a week, usually by phone, and I see her most Sundays or every other Sunday. My niece and nephew call me Auntie Raki, and I try to show up for birthdays, school events, and Saturday outings when I can. I also have aunties and cousins who are part of my support system. We are the kind of family where someone might irritate you, but if there is a hospital visit or a bill problem, people start making calls.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk to first when something stressful happens?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom, unless it is business-related. For business stress I call my friend Tasha because she tells me the truth quickly.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your brother's family?
follow_ups.response: Probably two or three times a month, more if there is a birthday, cookout, or my mom asks everybody to come over.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is my mom Angela, my dad Robert, and my brother Marcus. I am closest with my mom and brother, and with my dad it is respectful but a little more reserved.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents live together?
follow_ups.response: No, they separated years ago and live separately in Indianapolis.

follow_ups.question: Do you help either parent regularly?
follow_ups.response: I help my mom with errands and appointments sometimes, especially if she asks me to go with her.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are Tasha, who works in nonprofit community programs, and Monique, who is a nurse. We have a group text that is active almost every day, and we try to do dinner or jazz once a month. I also have friends from yoga, a running group, and the Indianapolis Canoe Club paddle-boarding group. I have dated, but I am single right now by choice. I want partnership eventually, but I am careful about who gets close because my work already takes a lot of emotional energy.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually spend time with friends?
follow_ups.response: We meet at coffee shops, jazz lounges, City Market, or somebody's kitchen. I like places where you can actually talk.

follow_ups.question: How do your friends support you?
follow_ups.response: They remind me to rest, send me business resources, and check me when I overthink something.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Indianapolis, in the 46218 area on the near east side. It is a mix of older homes, small apartment buildings, churches, corner stores, and families who have been here a long time. There are also vacant lots and places that need investment. I like that I know some neighbors by name and that people look out from their porches. At the same time, you can see how uneven development has been. There are community gardens, health fairs, and churches doing good work, but basic things like grocery access and safe sidewalks could be better.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go to regularly near home?
follow_ups.response: I go to a nearby pharmacy, a small grocery, my church when I attend, and sometimes a community center for health events.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few. Ms. Carolyn downstairs knows everybody, and I text one neighbor if packages are sitting out.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe in the daytime and cautious at night. I pay attention, park close to lights, and do not linger outside late by myself.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you cautious?
follow_ups.response: There have been car break-ins nearby and occasional arguments outside, so I just keep my routines smart.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially the older women on the block. They know who belongs and who does not.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is community memory and being close to my family and clients. The hard part is uneven services, noise sometimes, and wanting the neighborhood to get investment without pushing residents out.

follow_ups.question: What improvement would matter most?
follow_ups.response: Better grocery options and more safe, well-lit walking routes would make daily life healthier.

follow_ups.question: Would you like to stay there long term?
follow_ups.response: I would like to stay in Indianapolis, but eventually I want a quieter place or a small home.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live by myself in a rented one-bedroom apartment. No partner, children, roommate, or temporary guest lives with me. I like having a quiet home because my job is so people-focused. My apartment has a small living room, a kitchen where I cook a lot, a corner with my yoga mat, and a window shelf full of succulents.

follow_ups.question: Do you enjoy living alone?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes. It gives me peace and control over my routines.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone have a key to your place?
follow_ups.response: My mom has a spare key, and my friend Tasha knows where the backup is for emergencies.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me permanently.

follow_ups.question: Any overnight guests recently?
follow_ups.response: No, not recently.

follow_ups.question: Do family members ever stay for more than a night?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. My place is small.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one stays here regularly. A friend might crash on the couch after a late event once in a while.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a year.

follow_ups.question: Is that usually planned?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I like to know ahead of time.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one in care or hospitalized?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week is structured but not identical every day. Monday is lighter, usually laundry, scheduling, billing, grocery planning, and a yoga class. Tuesday through Saturday are my main massage days, with clients from late morning into evening. I run early two or three mornings a week because I am training for a half marathon. On Thursdays I often do paperwork after dinner, and on Saturdays I might see clients until mid-afternoon, then meet friends or family. Sunday is usually church, meal prep, stretching, and calling my mom.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up?
follow_ups.response: Around 5:45 or 6:00 on run days, closer to 7:00 on lighter days.

follow_ups.question: What is one thing you do almost every night?
follow_ups.response: I check the next day's schedule, set out clothes, and write a short journal note.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a licensed massage therapist. I rent treatment space part-time at a small wellness studio and also do some mobile sessions for regular clients. My hours are usually Tuesday through Friday from about 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., with breaks between sessions, and Saturdays from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. I do assessment, hands-on massage, notes, cleaning, scheduling, billing, and follow-up texts. Some weeks I also volunteer at a community health fair or teach a short stress-reduction workshop.

follow_ups.question: How many clients do you usually see in a day?
follow_ups.response: Four to six is ideal. More than that wears out my hands and shoulders.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of clients come to you?
follow_ups.response: A mix: nurses, teachers, warehouse workers, runners, older women with chronic pain, and people dealing with stress.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my mom with some errands and appointment reminders, and I keep close track of my own business paperwork. I do continuing education hours for my license. I also maintain my little succulent garden, cook most of my meals, and do a Sunday budget check. Spiritually, I try to meditate most mornings, even if it is only ten minutes.

follow_ups.question: What business task takes the most time?
follow_ups.response: Client notes and scheduling. I am careful because health history and boundaries matter.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually cook for the week?
follow_ups.response: Quinoa bowls with collards, roasted sweet potatoes, salmon or beans, and sometimes jalapeno cornbread.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is training more seriously for a half marathon. I moved my runs to sunrise because evening runs were too easy to skip after client work. I also started blocking one afternoon a week for planning the wellness center idea instead of trying to squeeze it in at midnight. That has helped my anxiety because the dream feels more like a project.

follow_ups.question: What day do you block for planning?
follow_ups.response: Usually Monday afternoon from about 2:00 to 5:00.

follow_ups.question: What does half-marathon training look like right now?
follow_ups.response: Two shorter weekday runs, one longer Saturday or Sunday run, plus yoga and mobility work.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids. I do help with my niece and nephew sometimes, but I am not their daily caregiver.

follow_ups.question: When do you help with your niece and nephew?
follow_ups.response: Mostly occasional Saturdays or when my brother and sister-in-law need help during family events.

follow_ups.question: Do they have activities you attend?
follow_ups.response: My niece has dance recitals sometimes, and I try to go when my schedule allows.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally, I have not had serious trouble with law enforcement. I have been pulled over twice, once for a taillight and once for speeding, and both times I felt tense even though nothing major happened. As a Black woman, I am very aware of how quickly an ordinary stop can feel unsafe. I keep my license and insurance organized, hands visible, voice calm. That is not because I think I did something wrong; it is because I know the history.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you how to handle traffic stops?
follow_ups.response: My parents and older cousins. It was one of those talks Black families have early.

follow_ups.question: Have police been involved in your neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Yes, they come through for noise, domestic disputes, or break-ins, but I usually keep distance.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: One that stands out is seeing police respond harshly to teenagers hanging near a store when I was younger. It stayed with me because the kids were loud, but they were still kids.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me think about discretion and how some neighborhoods get treated like problems.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police yourself?
follow_ups.response: Only once for a possible break-in in the building. I felt conflicted but wanted people safe.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a cousin who was arrested years ago for a drug-related charge, and that affected the family because getting back to stable work afterward was hard for him.

follow_ups.question: Are you close with that cousin?
follow_ups.response: We are not close day to day, but I see him at family gatherings.

follow_ups.question: What did you notice after his arrest?
follow_ups.response: The record followed him. Housing and jobs became harder even after he was trying to do right.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most local elections, though I have missed a primary before. Local elections matter to me because city council, prosecutors, school boards, and public health decisions touch daily life. I usually read candidate questionnaires and ask friends what they have heard. I am not the loudest political person online, but I do vote.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually early if I can, because my client schedule can change.

follow_ups.question: What issues decide your vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care access, neighborhood investment, reproductive rights, policing, and small business support.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left to progressive, especially on health care, racial justice, reproductive rights, and economic opportunity. I usually vote Democratic, but I do not think any party is perfect. My politics come from seeing how systems show up in bodies. When people cannot afford care, work two jobs, live near environmental stress, or carry racial stress every day, that is not just personal choice. I believe in personal responsibility too, but people need fair conditions to make healthy choices. I want government to be accountable and practical: fund clinics, improve public transit, support small businesses, keep neighborhoods safe without criminalizing residents, and invest in schools. I am also skeptical of performative politics. I care less about slogans and more about whether people can pay rent, get therapy, walk safely, and be treated with dignity.

follow_ups.question: Where do those views come from most?
follow_ups.response: Family, church, working with clients, and seeing health disparities in Black Indianapolis communities.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues where you are more moderate?
follow_ups.response: I am practical about business rules and taxes. I support regulation, but I notice when small operators get buried in paperwork.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on local policy and less impressed by national arguing. The pandemic, racial justice protests, and inflation made me look harder at public health and economic fragility. I used to think wellness was mostly individual habits, but now I see it as deeply connected to housing, work schedules, food access, and safety. I am also more protective of reproductive rights than I was when I was younger, because I have watched women carry heavy health and family burdens.

follow_ups.question: What local issue are you watching now?
follow_ups.response: Neighborhood development and whether it includes existing residents instead of just attracting new money.

follow_ups.question: Did your workplace experience change your politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Clients tell you what stress costs when they are lying on a table in pain.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot. Not because racism was new to me, but because the public attention made things that Black families have talked about forever suddenly visible to more people. It brought grief, anger, and fatigue. It also made me think about trauma in the nervous system, because watching videos and hearing stories over and over has a bodily effect. I had clients come in tense and exhausted from it.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it with clients?
follow_ups.response: Only when clients brought it up, but I held space and acknowledged that stress lives in the body.

follow_ups.question: What emotion was strongest for you?
follow_ups.response: A mix of grief and tiredness. Like, how many times do we have to explain basic humanity?

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as issues of dignity, accountability, and public health. Policing is part of it, but so are schools, housing, jobs, maternal health, and who gets believed when they say they are hurting. I support accountability for police misconduct and better investment in mental health responders. I also think Black communities deserve resources beyond crisis moments. We should not have to be injured publicly before people care.

follow_ups.question: What solution feels most important to you?
follow_ups.response: Independent accountability and more non-police crisis response for mental health situations.

follow_ups.question: How does this connect to your wellness work?
follow_ups.response: Chronic stress from racism affects sleep, blood pressure, pain, and trust. Bodywork cannot fix systems, but it can support healing.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about how race is both very visible and constantly denied. People will celebrate Black culture, music, food, and language, but still resist talking about power and policy. I also think about Black joy and not letting racism be the only story. My family, church traditions, jazz, cooking, and community care are sources of strength. So yes, I think about harm, but I also think about resilience and ownership.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see Black joy in your own life?
follow_ups.response: At family meals, jazz shows, church music, and when Black women clients feel seen and cared for.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about race with non-Black friends?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I do not make myself available for every debate. I protect my peace.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I talked with family and friends, attended one peaceful local march, donated a small amount to a bail fund, and shared voter information. Mostly I focused on community care and keeping conversations grounded.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel safe at the march?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, but I stayed with friends and left before it got late.

follow_ups.question: What did you post online?
follow_ups.response: Voting deadlines, local candidate information, and a few articles from sources I trusted.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends were engaged but tired. Tasha was very active with community meetings, Monique was dealing with hospital stress and racial disparities in health care, and my mom watched the news but sometimes had to turn it off. My brother was protective of his kids and had more direct conversations with them about police. In my circle, nobody was unaffected, but people responded according to their capacity.

follow_ups.question: How did your mother talk about it?
follow_ups.response: She connected it to things she saw growing up and said, 'This is not new; cameras are new.'

follow_ups.question: Did it change family conversations?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around what we tell children and how to keep hope without being naive.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say I am healthy, but I manage stress and anxiety carefully. My body is strong from yoga, running, and massage work, but my hands, wrists, shoulders, and low back need attention because of my job. I eat pretty well most of the time and cook at home. I have a primary care doctor, and I try not to ignore preventive care. Sleep is the thing that gets shaky when I am worried.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any diagnosed condition?
follow_ups.response: I have been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, and I manage it with therapy tools, exercise, meditation, and routines.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when your body hurts from work?
follow_ups.response: I stretch, use heat, trade massage with another therapist sometimes, and reduce clients if I need to.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy because health is part of my identity and work. I know how to move, stretch, cook, and read my body's signals. It is hard because being self-employed means inconsistent income, no employer health plan, and pressure to take clients even when I need rest. Stress makes me want to over-plan instead of sleep.

follow_ups.question: What habit helps the most?
follow_ups.response: Morning movement. Even twenty minutes changes my whole nervous system.

follow_ups.question: What gets in the way most often?
follow_ups.response: Late cancellations, money worries, and trying to fit paperwork into evenings.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The biggest thing was a wrist and forearm overuse flare-up last year. It scared me because my hands are my livelihood. I went to my doctor, did some physical therapy exercises, changed my body mechanics, and started spacing deep-tissue clients more carefully. Emotionally, I also had a stretch of anxiety where I woke up with racing thoughts about money and the future. I went back to therapy for a few sessions and tightened up my routines.

follow_ups.question: Did the wrist problem keep you from working?
follow_ups.response: I reduced appointments for about two weeks, but I did not fully stop.

follow_ups.question: What did physical therapy teach you?
follow_ups.response: Strengthening, pacing, and using my body weight instead of muscling through with my hands.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The wrist flare-up affected work because I had to limit certain techniques. Anxiety can affect work too if I do not manage it, mostly by making me overthink scheduling or finances.

follow_ups.question: Have you had to cancel clients for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: A few times, but I try to reschedule quickly and communicate clearly.

follow_ups.question: Does it affect family care?
follow_ups.response: Not heavily, since I do not have children, but I may have less energy for errands with my mom.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. My mom has high blood pressure, and I pay attention to that. She is pretty independent, but I remind her about appointments and medication refills. I also had an aunt with diabetes complications, and that shaped how I think about prevention in Black families. It is part of why I want affordable wellness education, not just treatment after things get serious.

follow_ups.question: Do you go to appointments with your mom?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially if she wants another set of ears.

follow_ups.question: Does your family talk openly about health?
follow_ups.response: More than we used to. Older relatives sometimes kept things private, but my generation pushes questions.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have not gone without urgent care, but I have delayed things like therapy or dental work because of cost. Since I am self-employed, insurance is a monthly bill I feel. Finding providers who listen is another issue. My mom has Medicare-age coverage now, so that helps her, but navigating appointments and bills can still be confusing.

follow_ups.question: What care did you delay most recently?
follow_ups.response: Dental work. I waited a few months before scheduling because I wanted to know what insurance would cover.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel respected by providers?
follow_ups.response: Usually, but I am alert. I ask questions and write things down.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, if you include massage, yoga, herbal teas, prayer, and home remedies. My grandmother believed in ginger tea, Epsom salt baths, and prayer before anything else. I use evidence-based massage and I respect traditional practices, but I do not tell people to skip medical care. I think the best approach is integrative: know when a doctor is needed and also support the body with movement, rest, food, and community.

follow_ups.question: What home remedy do you still use?
follow_ups.response: Ginger tea with lemon when I feel run down, and Epsom salt baths for soreness.

follow_ups.question: Do clients ask you about alternative care?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and I stay in my scope. I can talk about stress and body mechanics, not diagnose.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink occasionally, usually a glass of natural wine with dinner or at a jazz night, but not as my main coping tool. When I am stressed, I am more likely to clean, make lists, cook, run, or get quiet. I have learned that alcohol makes my sleep worse, so I am careful.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three times a month, sometimes less.

follow_ups.question: What do you reach for instead during stress?
follow_ups.response: Peppermint tea, a hot shower, journaling, or a walk.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana regularly and I do not use other substances. I take over-the-counter ibuprofen occasionally if my wrist or shoulder is inflamed, and I use magnesium at night sometimes. I have not taken prescription anxiety medication recently, though I have discussed options with my doctor. My most recent pain-medication use was probably ibuprofen after a long client day and a training run landed on the same week.

follow_ups.question: Why avoid regular marijuana use?
follow_ups.response: It is not really my thing, and I like to keep my mind clear for work.

follow_ups.question: How often do you take ibuprofen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, not daily.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay for an individual health insurance plan and budget for copays and dental costs. It is not cheap, but I treat it as necessary. My mom uses her coverage and I help her understand bills when needed. For wellness, we do a lot ourselves: cooking, walking, church support, and checking in on each other.

follow_ups.question: Do medical bills stress you financially?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially dental or anything out of network.

follow_ups.question: Do you use an HSA or savings for care?
follow_ups.response: I keep a small health cushion in savings, but it is not as big as I want.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I got COVID vaccines and boosters, and I get a flu shot most years, especially because I work close to people's bodies.

follow_ups.question: Were you hesitant at any point?
follow_ups.response: I had questions at first like a lot of people, but I read credible information and talked to medical people I trusted.

follow_ups.question: Does your family agree?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though some relatives are more skeptical than I am.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my primary care doctor, nurses I know personally, the CDC for basic guidance, and local health department updates. I also pay attention to Black physicians and public health educators because they often explain concerns in a culturally aware way. I avoid random viral posts unless I can trace them to a real medical source.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss vaccines with clients?
follow_ups.response: Only if it comes up, and I do not argue. I share that I rely on medical sources.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get local health updates?
follow_ups.response: Marion County public health information and sometimes community clinic newsletters.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year has been a mix of proud and stretched thin. I feel proud because my client base is steadier, I am training for something physical, and I have a clearer vision for the wellness center. But I also feel pressure: money, family health, being single at 37, and wondering if I am behind some imaginary timeline. My anxiety shows up as planning, checking, and replaying conversations. The good part is I know myself better now. I can tell when I need rest before I crash.

follow_ups.question: What has made you feel proudest recently?
follow_ups.response: A client told me she felt listened to for the first time in months. That stayed with me.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel most anxious?
follow_ups.response: Late at night when bills, business ideas, and family worries all show up at once.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last winter I had a week where three clients canceled, my car needed work, and my wrist was hurting. I remember sitting at my kitchen table with unopened mail and feeling like I was one bad month away from losing momentum. I called Tasha and cried, which I do not do easily. She came over with soup, helped me sort the bills, and made me list what was actually urgent. The next day I called the mechanic, adjusted my schedule, and booked a therapy session.

follow_ups.question: What helped most in that moment?
follow_ups.response: Having someone sit with me and separate fear from facts.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you handle stress now?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I ask for help sooner and do not open bills at midnight anymore.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I struggle with anxiety, specifically generalized anxiety. It is manageable, but it is real. I worry about finances, health, making mistakes, and whether I am doing enough. I have had low moods, but I would not say depression is my main struggle. Therapy, movement, prayer, and routines help me stay grounded.

follow_ups.question: How long has anxiety been part of your life?
follow_ups.response: Probably since childhood, though I did not have language for it until adulthood.

follow_ups.question: What does anxiety look like physically?
follow_ups.response: Tight chest, clenched jaw, shallow breathing, and sometimes stomach knots.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My family has had stress too. My mom worries about health and money, my brother worries about raising Black children safely, and everybody is tired from prices going up. We cope with humor, food, prayer, and checking in.

follow_ups.question: Who carries stress quietly?
follow_ups.response: My brother. He jokes a lot, but I know he carries pressure.

follow_ups.question: Do family gatherings help?
follow_ups.response: Yes, even when they are loud. Being fed and known helps.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Spirituality is important to me. I was raised in the Black Baptist church, and I still identify as Christian, though I am not in church every Sunday like my grandmother was. I attend service maybe twice a month, more around holidays or family events. Prayer, gospel music, and the rhythm of church shaped how I understand care and community. I also practice meditation and yoga, so my spirituality is both traditional and body-based. I do not see those as contradictory. For me, God, breath, music, and community are all connected to healing.

follow_ups.question: What church tradition feels most meaningful?
follow_ups.response: Call-and-response, testimony, and the music. That is where you feel people carrying each other.

follow_ups.question: Do you belong to a specific church now?
follow_ups.response: I still attend a Baptist church in Indianapolis, but I would call myself a regular visitor more than a committee person.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Instagram the most, partly personal and partly professional. I post appointment openings, wellness tips, stretches, books I am reading, food I cook, and sometimes clips from jazz nights. Facebook is more for family, church people, and community events. I do not use X much. I try not to scroll first thing in the morning because it spikes my anxiety. I like social media as a tool, but I have to put boundaries around it.

follow_ups.question: How often do you post for your business?
follow_ups.response: Two or three times a week if I am organized, less when I am busy.

follow_ups.question: What accounts do you follow?
follow_ups.response: Massage educators, Black wellness professionals, local restaurants, jazz venues, running pages, and psychology authors.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: I do not usually ask social media for emotional or financial support. I go to close friends and family first. I might share a community fundraiser for someone else, though.

follow_ups.question: Why not ask online?
follow_ups.response: I am private, and I do not like feeling exposed when I am already stressed.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever received business support online?
follow_ups.response: Yes, people book through Instagram or share my posts, and that helps.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: My stress went up with business costs and car expenses, but my coping is better than it used to be. I now schedule recovery time, limit late-night scrolling, journal, and ask for help sooner.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy is newest?
follow_ups.response: Blocking Monday afternoons for planning and not treating every idea like an emergency.

follow_ups.question: What strategy did you stop using?
follow_ups.response: I stopped pretending that making another list is the same as resting.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I am a licensed massage therapist. My work starts before a client gets on the table because I review their health history, pain patterns, goals, contraindications, and stress level. I do deep tissue, myofascial release, sports massage, lymphatic drainage, and relaxation work depending on the person. I keep session notes, handle scheduling and billing, clean the room carefully, wash linens, and communicate boundaries. The most important duty is listening well and applying the right technique safely. A massage is not just rubbing a sore spot; it is assessment, pressure control, anatomy, trust, and follow-up care.

follow_ups.question: What session type do you do most often?
follow_ups.response: Deep tissue mixed with myofascial release for neck, shoulders, low back, and hip tension.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest about the job?
follow_ups.response: Protecting my own body and managing the emotional weight people bring into the room.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Indianapolis, Indiana.

follow_ups.question: Same side of town?
follow_ups.response: Yes, east side Indianapolis.

follow_ups.question: What school area was that?
follow_ups.response: An Indianapolis public school area.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: No. By then I lived mainly with my mother. My father was involved but not living in the home.

follow_ups.question: Did you see your father regularly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but it was not the same as living together.

follow_ups.question: Was that transition hard?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but my mother kept the household steady.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: I lived with my mother and my younger brother Marcus.

follow_ups.question: Any grandparents in the home?
follow_ups.response: No, but my grandmother was around a lot.

follow_ups.question: Were cousins ever there?
follow_ups.response: They visited often but did not live with us.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: My dad completed high school and some vocational training.

follow_ups.question: What kind of training?
follow_ups.response: Maintenance and building trades type training.

follow_ups.question: Did he value education?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially practical skills.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mom completed some college but did not finish a bachelor's degree.

follow_ups.question: Did she encourage college?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very much.

follow_ups.question: Was she proud of your associate degree?
follow_ups.response: Very proud.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my mom worked for pay while I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was she full time?
follow_ups.response: Most of the time, yes.

follow_ups.question: Did her work shape you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I learned organization and responsibility from her.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mom worked in health care administration, mostly scheduling, patient records, phones, and billing support. She was the person making sure appointments, paperwork, and insurance details did not fall through the cracks.

follow_ups.question: Did she work directly with patients?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by phone and front desk, not clinical care.

follow_ups.question: What skill did you learn from watching her?
follow_ups.response: How to stay calm with people who are worried or frustrated.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for medical offices and clinic settings in Indianapolis. They provided patient care, appointments, referrals, and billing, mostly everyday health services rather than hospital emergency care.

follow_ups.question: Was it a large organization?
follow_ups.response: Some offices were part of larger health systems, others felt smaller.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and I remember the phones, files, and waiting room energy.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my dad worked for pay while I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was his work steady?
follow_ups.response: Mostly steady, though there were changes.

follow_ups.question: Did he work with his hands?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad worked in building maintenance. He repaired things, handled basic plumbing and electrical issues, kept facilities running, and responded when something broke. He was good with tools and practical problem solving.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you any repair skills?
follow_ups.response: Small things, like checking breakers, tightening screws, and not panicking when something leaks.

follow_ups.question: Was he proud of hands-on work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, he believed useful skills give you independence.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for apartment complexes and commercial buildings. Those places provided housing or office space, and his job was to keep the buildings safe, functional, and presentable.

follow_ups.question: Did his job affect family time?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, because maintenance calls could happen after hours.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your view of labor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me respect work people only notice when it is not done.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I have finished or am close to finishing a bachelor's degree in holistic health. I want a small boutique wellness center in Indianapolis that feels warm but professional, with affordable massage, stress-management workshops, chronic pain support, and culturally responsive health education. I imagine a place where Black women, caregivers, workers, and elders feel respected instead of rushed. Personally, I hope I have more financial cushion, a healthier work pace, and maybe a partner who fits my life without shrinking it. I want to travel more too, especially a wellness road trip through the Southwest national parks. Mostly I want my life to feel rooted, useful, and spacious.

follow_ups.question: What would the wellness center be called?
follow_ups.response: I have played with the name Root & Rest Wellness, though I am not fully settled.

follow_ups.question: What would a typical day there look like?
follow_ups.response: Morning massage sessions, an afternoon workshop on stress or posture, and maybe an evening yoga or pain-care class.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value health, dignity, family, community, and peace. Not just peace as quiet, but peace as being able to breathe in your own life. I value work that helps people feel more at home in their bodies. I value my culture, the stories and meals and music that shaped me. And I value integrity: doing what I said I would do, even when nobody is watching.

follow_ups.question: Which value guides daily decisions most?
follow_ups.response: Integrity. It affects how I treat clients, spend money, and show up for family.

follow_ups.question: What gives you peace most reliably?
follow_ups.response: Morning yoga, Coltrane playing low, a clean kitchen, and knowing my people are okay.

summaries.behavioral_economist: Raki is organized, future-oriented, and loss-averse around financial and health shocks, using spreadsheets, budgeting apps, savings buckets, and routines to manage uncertainty (Q03, Q57, Q61). Her self-employment gives flexibility but also exposes her to income volatility, cancellations, and injury risk, shaping her careful emergency planning (Q78, Q81, Q82). Her consumption choices favor health, cultural meaning, and community identity, while discretionary dining and events are cut first when money tightens (Q60, Q81).
summaries.political_scientist: Raki is a fairly strong Democratic voter with center-left to progressive views on health care, racial justice, reproductive rights, economic opportunity, and local neighborhood investment (Q23, Q24, Q95, Q96). Her institutional trust is selective: she values public health, voting, and local policy, but is skeptical of performative politics and police practices that criminalize Black neighborhoods (Q24, Q26, Q27). Her civic identity is grounded in Indianapolis Black community life and a desire for practical, accountable public systems (Q08, Q108).
